title: How Comic Books: Live from SXSW
summary: Live recording at South by Southwest (SXSW) in Austin, Texas, before about a hundred people. Josh and Chuck open with banter about Nicolas Cage's stolen Action Comics No. 1 and its recovery, then cover comic book history: the Adventures of Obadiah Oldbuck (1842) as an early comic, the Yellow Kid and the origin of "yellow journalism," the shift to original content at Eastern Color and DC (New Fun Comics No. 1), Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman and William Marston, comics in World War II, Spire Christian Comics and Hans the Girl Who Loved the Swastika, Fredric Wertham's Seduction of the Innocent and the Comics Code Authority, underground comics, Will Eisner and the graphic novel, Marvel and Stan Lee's flawed heroes, manga sales, comic artists and creators' lists, and Art Spiegelman's Maus. The episode ends with audience questions about topic selection (including Scientology), research methods, the show's schedule, and a premiere party for their TV pilot.

segments.title: Opening banter and Nicolas Cage's stolen comic
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck greet the SXSW audience in Austin and joke about the room size. Josh tells the story of Nicolas Cage's stolen Action Comics No. 1, recovered about ten years later from a storage-unit auction purchase, and a movie planned about the incident. They introduce the comic book topic and say they are not experts.
topics: Nicolas Cage Action Comics No. 1 theft

segments.title: Defining comics and sequential art
segments.summary: The hosts discuss what a comic book is, the layout of panels and gutters, the reading flow of panels, and comics as sequential art. They call comics a pure American art form alongside jazz and the mystery novel.

segments.title: Obadiah Oldbuck and the Yellow Kid
segments.summary: The hosts describe The Adventures of Obadiah Oldbuck, generally credited as the first comic book, created by Rodolphe Töpffer in 1842. They then cover the Yellow Kid as the first humorous comic strip with speech balloons, and how the term yellow journalism came from the strip's association with a Hearst newspaper.

segments.title: Eastern Color, DC Comics and Superman
segments.summary: Eastern Color printed reprinted newspaper comics, which Procter and Gamble gave away. The company then moved to original material, leading to DC's New Fun Comics No. 1. Issue six introduced Superman by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, described as the first costumed superhero. The hosts also mention a George Reeves anecdote about a kid with a gun.

segments.title: Golden Age heroes, Batman and Wonder Woman
segments.summary: The hosts cover Detective Comics and Batman, the long-running Detective series, and Wonder Woman's creation by William Marston, who also helped invent the lie detector. They note Marston's unconventional home life.

segments.title: World War II comics and Disney
segments.summary: Superhero comics were popular during World War II, with characters fighting Hitler before the US entered the war, such as Captain America's first cover. Disney comics, including Uncle Scrooge McDuck, were also very popular. The American government sent comics to troops, creating a new adult readership.

segments.title: Spire Christian Comics and Hans the Girl Who Loved the Swastika
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Spire Christian Comics, created by cartoonist Al Hartley after his conversion, and publisher Fleming H. Revell's support for the line. They describe the comic Hans the Girl Who Loved the Swastika, based on a real story, and note the character does not age.
topics: Hans the Girl Who Loved the Swastika

segments.title: Seduction of the Innocent and the Comics Code Authority
segments.summary: Psychiatrist Fredric Wertham's book The Seduction of the Innocent claimed comics harmed children, prompting a comic book burning in New York and parental backlash. The industry created the self-imposed Comics Code Authority. The hosts read highlights of the code, including rules on crime, violence, profanity, religion, and depiction of women. The code drove creators toward underground comics.

segments.title: Underground comics, graphic novels and Marvel
segments.summary: Underground comix, including R. Crumb and Fritz the Cat, took on mature themes. Will Eisner's A Contract with God is considered an early graphic novel. The hosts discuss Watchmen, Maus, Frank Miller, and Batman's changing image. Stan Lee's Marvel introduced flawed heroes and a shared universe.

segments.title: Manga, top artists and Maus
segments.summary: The hosts note manga's large sales in Japan and North America. They describe the team behind a comic (writer, penciler, inker, colorist, letterer) and discuss a list of top artists including Jack Kirby, Neal Adams, Harvey Kurtzman, Lou Fine, and Frank Frazetta. They then describe Art Spiegelman's Maus, which won a Pulitzer Prize special award.

segments.title: Sponsor and promo reads
segments.summary: A short sponsor read and promotional mention of a video podcast, with a note about the Stuff You Should Know site search for comic books.

segments.title: Audience Q&A: how topics are chosen and Scientology
segments.summary: Audience members ask how Josh and Chuck became co-hosts, and why topics such as Scientology have not been covered. The hosts say Scientology is litigious and that sources are mostly hearsay.

segments.title: Audience Q&A: Guatemala episodes and research methods
segments.summary: A listener from Guatemala asks about material left out of the Guatemala episodes. Another audience member asks how the hosts validate research; they answer that they mostly rely on HowStuffWorks articles plus cross-checking multiple sources, with occasional library visits, such as for the Elizabeth Báthory article.

segments.title: Audience Q&A: schedule and TV pilot premiere
segments.summary: An audience member asks about the hosts' schedule. They say they record two to four episodes weekly and release two, maintaining a backlog, and mention a TV pilot premiere party at an Austin Irish pub, with the pilot funded by the Science Channel.

segments.title: Closing and contact information
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank the audience, give Twitter and Facebook contact details and an email address, and promote the video podcast Stuff from the Future before a closing ad.
